title: Dhruva's Determination
summary: A little prince, pushed away from his father's lap, goes to the forest and finds something greater than a throne.
body:
Dhruva was a small boy, about five years old, the son of King Uttānapāda. One day he tried to climb onto his father's lap, but his stepmother Suruci, the king's favourite queen, pushed him away. She told him that he had no right to sit there unless he worshipped the Lord and took birth from her own womb.

Hurt, Dhruva ran to his mother Sunīti. She did not tell him to seek revenge. She told him that if he wanted a place higher than any his father could give, he should take shelter of the Supreme Lord.

Dhruva left for the forest. There the sage Nārada met him, tested his resolve, and tried to talk him out of it. When Dhruva stayed firm, Nārada taught him how to worship the Lord and sent him to Madhuvana on the bank of the Yamunā.

Dhruva practised severe austerities, and the Lord appeared before him. Seeing the Lord, he felt there was nothing more he wanted. The Lord blessed him with a long reign and, afterwards, a permanent abode called Dhruvaloka.

title: Prahlāda and Lord Nṛsiṁha
summary: A boy who would not stop remembering the Lord, and the Lord who appeared from a pillar in answer.
body:
Hiraṇyakaśipu, a powerful demon king, hated Lord Viṣṇu. His own young son Prahlāda was devoted to the Lord from childhood, having heard Nārada's teachings even before he was born.

At school, Prahlāda spoke to his classmates about devotion and told them to begin early. When his father heard of it, he tried to turn the boy away, and then tried to harm him in many ways. Prahlāda remained peaceful and unafraid through all of it.

In a final confrontation Hiraṇyakaśipu demanded to know where this Viṣṇu was. Prahlāda replied that the Lord is everywhere. Mocking him, the king struck a pillar of the assembly hall.

The Lord then appeared from the pillar as Nṛsiṁha, with the body of a man and the head of a lion, at twilight, at the threshold of the hall. In this form he fulfilled the words of Hiraṇyakaśipu's boon and ended his tyranny.

Prahlāda then offered prayers. When the Lord offered him a boon, Prahlāda asked only that he never be bound by material desires.

title: Ambarīṣa and Durvāsā
summary: A powerful sage grows angry at a devout king, and learns where real power lies.
body:
King Ambarīṣa was observing a year-long vow of Ekādaśī and Dvādaśī fasting. At the end of it, the sage Durvāsā arrived as a guest. Ambarīṣa invited him to eat, and Durvāsā went to bathe in the river but was delayed.

The time for breaking the fast was running out. On the advice of learned brāhmaṇas, Ambarīṣa sipped some water, which kept the vow without being a meal, and waited for the sage.

Durvāsā knew what had happened and became furious. He created a fierce being to destroy the king. Ambarīṣa did not move. The Lord's cakra, Sudarśana, destroyed the creature and then pursued Durvāsā across the universe.

Brahmā and Śiva could not help him. Lord Nārāyaṇa told him that he was under the control of his devotees and that Durvāsā should go to Ambarīṣa for forgiveness. Durvāsā returned and fell at his feet. Ambarīṣa, who had waited for him for a whole year without taking a proper meal, prayed to the cakra, and it withdrew. He then fed the sage with great respect.

title: Kṛṣṇa Lifts Govardhana
summary: When a storm threatens Vraja, a young Kṛṣṇa holds a whole hill above the people for seven days.
body:
The residents of Vraja were preparing their yearly offering to Indra, the king of the heavenly planets. The young Kṛṣṇa asked his father Nanda why they did this. After hearing the traditional reasons, Kṛṣṇa suggested that they should rather honour the cows, the brāhmaṇas, and Govardhana Hill, since it was the hill that fed their cows. The elders agreed.

Indra was angry at the loss of his offering and sent clouds of heavy rain upon Vraja. The people, frightened, ran to Kṛṣṇa.

Kṛṣṇa lifted Govardhana Hill with one hand and held it up like an umbrella. The people of Vraja along with their cows gathered beneath it, and Kṛṣṇa kept the hill in place for seven days until the storm exhausted itself.

Indra, humbled, stopped the rain, and later came to Kṛṣṇa to ask for forgiveness.

title: The Appearance of Kṛṣṇa
summary: At midnight in a locked prison in Mathurā, the Lord appears, and his father carries him across the Yamunā to safety.
body:
King Kaṁsa of Mathurā had been told by a heavenly voice at his sister Devakī's wedding that her eighth child would be the cause of his death. He imprisoned Devakī and her husband Vasudeva, and killed their children one by one.

At midnight, when the Lord was to appear as their eighth child, the sky was calm and the directions were peaceful. He first appeared before Devakī and Vasudeva in a four-armed form. At their request he became an ordinary-looking infant.

The prison doors opened by themselves and the guards fell asleep. Vasudeva carried the child through heavy rain and across the Yamunā, which made a way for him, to the village of Gokula. There he placed the baby beside Yaśodā, exchanged him for her newborn daughter, and returned to the prison.

title: Nārada's Previous Life
summary: The story of how the son of a maidservant became the great sage Nārada, through the association of saints.
body:
Nārada tells Vyāsadeva that in a previous life he was the son of a maidservant. She served a group of sages who stayed in the village during the four months of the rainy season.

As a small boy he did small services for the sages, ate the remnants of their food, and listened to their talks about the Lord. This purified him, and he grew attached to hearing about Kṛṣṇa.

When the sages were leaving, they gave him confidential instruction. Soon afterwards his mother died of a snakebite, and he accepted it as the Lord's mercy, freeing him from attachment. He went away to the north, sat down under a tree, and meditated on the Lord.

He had a brief vision of the Lord in his heart, but it disappeared. A voice told him that he would not see the Lord again in this life, but that his devotion would remain. At the end of that life, he left his body, and in a later creation he appeared as Nārada.

title: Nārada Instructs Vyāsa
summary: A sage who has written everything is still unsatisfied, until a visitor explains what is missing.
body:
Vyāsadeva had arranged the Vedas and written the Purāṇas and the Mahābhārata, but he felt something was still lacking. He sat on the bank of the Sarasvatī river, troubled.

Nārada arrived at his hermitage and told him that although he had described many things, he had not described the glories of the Lord directly and fully. Nārada advised him to do so.

Vyāsa then meditated in deep concentration, saw the Lord and the energy that covers the souls, and composed the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam. He taught it to his son Śukadeva.

title: Parīkṣit and Śukadeva
summary: A king with seven days left to live asks the one question that matters, and receives the Bhāgavatam as the answer.
body:
King Parīkṣit, thirsty after a hunt, entered the hermitage of the sage Śamīka, who was deep in meditation and did not respond. Annoyed, the king placed a dead snake around the sage's neck and left.

The sage's young son heard about it and cursed the king to be bitten by the snake-bird Takṣaka and die in seven days. When Parīkṣit learned of this, he accepted it as a sign to turn away from the world. He gave up his kingdom, and sat on the bank of the Gaṅgā, fasting.

Many great sages came to see him. Śukadeva Gosvāmī arrived and Parīkṣit asked him what a person who is about to die should hear and do.

In reply, Śukadeva narrated the Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam for seven days.

title: The Gītā at Kurukṣetra
summary: On the eve of battle, a confused warrior puts down his bow, and Kṛṣṇa begins to teach.
body:
Two great armies stood ready on the field of Kurukṣetra. Arjuna asked Kṛṣṇa, who was his charioteer, to drive the chariot into the space between the lines so that he could see who he would be fighting.

He saw teachers, relatives and friends on the other side. Overcome with grief and confusion, he set down his bow and said that he could not fight.

Kṛṣṇa then began to teach him. He began with the difference between the body, which changes, and the soul, which is eternal, and went on to speak about duty, knowledge, and devotion. The teachings, in about seven hundred verses, are known as the Bhagavad-gītā.

title: The Seven Temples of Vṛndāvana
summary: How seven Vṛndāvana temples preserve the memory of the Gosvāmīs and their Gauḍīya lineage.
body:
In Vṛndāvana, seven holy temples are especially associated with the early Gauḍīya Gosvāmīs. Each keeps a deity before the community and recalls the teacher who served that līlā-sthāna.

Madana-mohana is linked with Sanātana Gosvāmī, Govindadeva with Rūpa Gosvāmī, Gopīnātha with Mādhupandita through Gadādhara Paṇḍita, and Rādhā-Dāmodara with Jīva Gosvāmī. Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja wrote Caitanya-caritāmṛta at Rādhā-Dāmodara in his later years.

Rādhā-Ramaṇa is linked with Gopāla Bhaṭṭa Gosvāmī, Rādhā-Śyāmasundara with Śyāmānanda through Hṛdaya Caitanya and Gauridāsa Paṇḍita, and Rādhā-Gokulānanda with Lokanātha Gosvāmī. Bhūgarbha Gosvāmī, Lokanātha's close associate, helped discover and establish early Vraja bhajana sites.

Jayadeva belonged to an earlier century and was not historically in this paramparā, yet the Gīta Govinda was deeply relished by Śrī Caitanya in Jagannātha Purī and became a source for the rāgānugā mood later embraced in Gauḍīya teaching.

This entry remain a draft. Details marked 'traditionally accepted' are kept exactly as received and still need review.

title: The Sixteen Deities of Vajranābha
summary: Traditional traditions of sixteen deities installed across Vraja by Vajranābha.
body:
Vraja tradition, including purāṇic descriptions linked to the Ādi-Varāha Purāṇa, says that Vajranābha installed at least sixteen deities at sacred places across Vraja Maṇḍala.

Four principal Devas: Śrī Govindadeva in Vṛndāvana, later taken to Jaipur; Śrī Keśavadeva in Mathurā; Śrī Harideva beside Mānasī-gaṅgā near Govardhana; and Śrī Baladeva, also called Dauji, in Mahāvana.

Four Gopāla forms: Śrī Sākṣi-Gopāla in Vṛndāvana; Śrī Madana-Mohana in Vṛndāvana, later Karauli; Śrī Gopinātha in Vṛndāvana, later Jaipur; and Śrī Śrīnātha at Aniyora near Govardhana.

Four Śiva liṅgas (Dik-pālas): Bhūteśvara in Mathurā, Gopīśvara in Vṛndāvana, Cakreśvara at Govardhana, and Kāmeśvara in Kāmyavana.

Four Devīs: Yogamāyā at Yoga-pīṭha in Vṛndāvana, Vṛndā-devī in Kāmyavana, Manasī-devī at Govardhana, and Pātāla-devī in Mathurā.

These forests — Mahāvana, Vṛndāvana, Kāmyavana, Madhuvana, Bahulāvana, Khadiravana and others — form the Vṛndāvana Maṇḍala where Vajranābha is said to have placed many of these mūrtis.

This is a draft summary of traditional lore and still needs review.

title: Gaura-līlā and Kṛṣṇa-līlā
summary: Two settings, one Lord: how Vraja is recognized in the Gaura pastimes.
body:
Many Vaiṣṇavas understand the pastimes of Śrī Caitanya and the pastimes of Śrī Kṛṣṇa as two horizons of one divine life. The Gaura pastimes unfold in Navadvīpa and Māyāpura; the Vraja pastimes unfold in Vṛndāvana and along the Yamunā. The same Lord is present in both, and His intimate associates appear in both settings.

The Pañca-tattva are understood as Kṛṣṇa and His immediate expansions: Caitanya as Kṛṣṇa with Rādhā's mood, Nityānanda as Balarāma, Advaita as Mahā-Viṣṇu and Sadāśiva, Gadādhara as the internal potency, and Śrīvāsa as Nārada among the devotees. The Gosvāmīs and the many branches around them are similarly connected with figures and friends in Vraja.

This way of seeing does not flatten the two līlās into one story. It lets a visitor recognize Vraja in Gaura's company and Gaura in Vraja's memory. The correspondences are traditional identifications, kept here as draft notes.

title: The Cowherd Boys of Vraja
summary: Kṛṣṇa's boy companions in Vraja, gathered for browsing.
body:
Kṛṣṇa's boy companions in Vraja form a wide circle of friends, servants, well-wishers and intimate confidants. Some are called sakhas, and some are remembered by the distinctive service they offered while tending cattle beside Him.

This story gathers the names recorded for those companions so they can be browsed together. The entries are short drafts; fuller notes can be added as each name is reviewed.

title: The Gopīs of Vraja
summary: The gopīs of Vraja, including the aṣṭa-sakhīs and mañjarīs.
body:
The gopīs of Vraja are remembered as Kṛṣṇa's intimate companions, with Śrīmatī Rādhārāṇī at the centre. The aṣṭa-sakhīs and the mañjarīs are named groups within this wider circle.

This story gathers those names together for browsing. The entries are short drafts; fuller notes can be added as each name is reviewed.
